The white sea stretched out before us. We'd made it, we'd made it to the eastern tip.

The research crew began unloading the trucks and setting up base camp, I went over to help them. We decided we'd have some drinks and settle for the day, and venture on in the morning. I went with Luke to scout out the drop. It was just as foreboding as it was everywhere else around Aeros. A sheer cliff that dropped hundreds of feet before being swallowed up by the white sea. Nobody knew how far it was in total, or if it stopped at all.

The rest of the drop had a much more violent white sea, with waves and vortexes that made the expeditions there too dangerous, this was the calmest point, and the conditions were looking perfect. The sea seemed calm and quiet. You could almost mistake it for clouds or mist. What the sea was actually made of was yet to be confirmed. A few containers of the stuff had been brought up from other places on the drop, but as soon as it got close to the top it turned clear and vanished from within the containers. It seems the only way to observe it close up is to head down to it.

The night was nice, a last party at the end of the world before we press on tomorrow. Looking out over the sea at the end of the world by a campfire, with surprising quantities of beer.

The sun was harsh the next morning, reflecting off the sea so that even looking to the north would hurt your eyes. We would be descending the south face, getting shade from the sun. The cage had been set up, the cables were ready and checked, and me and Luke prepared ourselves for the descent.

We'd had training, keep close to the wall, if the wall moves in you need to hammer in loops for the cables so that you can stay by the wall. If you move too far out you hang in free space and the sea batters you about when you have no chance to keep in control. Hopefully that wouldn't be an issue, with the sea as calm as it was, but the goings on under the surface couldn't be accounted for from here.

We climbed into the cage, checked our equipment one last time, stocked up on loops to hammer into the rock, even food and supplies enough to last us a few days should we be stranded. We began our descent.

50 ft, add a couple of loops, feed the cable through, carry on down.

100 ft, add a couple of loops, feed the cable through, carry on down.

150 ft, add a couple of loops, feed the cable through, carry on down.

200 ft, add a couple of loops, feed the cable through, carry on down.

At around 225 feet we started to reach the white sea. The low waves buffeted you like incredibly heavy air. I dread to think what it would be like if the sea wasn't so calm. The cage bashed against the wall now, so we added another set of loops early.

Vision was a problem as we descended further. People had already confirmed that you could breathe normally in the sea, but it obscured vision so you were limited to a few feet, sometimes less. The cage hammered against the wall, it had wheels to let it descend in contact with the cliff face, but they didn't do much to take away the shocks. We were using loops far more often now. We were easily 50ft below the start of the sea now.

The wall began to curve inwards. This was probably the worst news we could have. This meant hanging away from the wall unless you used loops every 10ft or so. The sea seemed to be as calm as it was before (which was still not calm enough for our liking) but the air almost had a texture now. You had to push your limbs through it to move, breathing was a strain as the air was thicker and took more effort to inhale.

It had been about 2 hours now. And we must have only made another 150ft in the last hour of that. Taking up to a total depth of around 500. The guys on the surface knew exactly, they had stripes on the cable at different intervals. But we were going blind. We continued descending, but so slowly now with the wall's tilt forcing us to a crawl.

The sound of the hammer is the only thing in our heads now. As we put in what must be our 50th set of loops. The rock seems harder here, making the tilt of the drop even worse. The white chalk has given way to a harder grey rock. We take a chunk of it as a sample. It shimmers slightly.

The sea has now continued for about 500ft from when it started. The air keeps getting heavier and heavier, breathing is a difficult task now, like someone is covering your mouth with a thick cloth. It's also getting darker now. The light can only diffuse down so far, and though it's not that bad, it is noticeable, and may be a problem later.

The wall stopped tilting inwards now, it was a sigh of relief and we started making much more progress. The air had even started thinning now, and we could see just a little bit better. We could now do about 25ft per set of loops again, which sped our descent. We decided to stop for a break and some food.

That was when something very strange happened.

It was like a bird call, but nothing had ever been seen going into the sea, or coming out of it. We only heard it because we had stopped. It was soon followed by another, slightly different this time, like an answer to the first one's call. We had no idea what to make of it, and though we waited for quite a while we heard nothing else like it, so we carried on.

The wall started tilting the other way.

The sea was still getting thinner.

Soon, we seemed to reach it's edge. It ended like it began, this was like an inverted version of the sea's surface.

Below us we saw the cliff, stretching maybe another 100ft, and beyond that a dense woodland. The bird sounds we heard earlier seemed to come from strange bat-like creatures, they weaved in and out of the sea, before diving down into the woods again.

The light levels had reached what perfectly matched the description twilight. So after deciding on a name for it, we proceeded to descend the rest of the way to the twilight forest.

The excitement of it is still flowing through me. We sent up the capsule, telling the people back up at the top of the drop what we had seen, the cage is almost a shuttle now, and we've set up another camp at the base of the cliff. The drop ended up to be about 1200ft in total, with the loops in place already the whole journey takes about 3 hours.

News of our discovery will have reached the city of Tellac by now, they'll probably want to find some way to make getting down here easier, send more researchers, and eventually there may even be a colonization attempt down here.

The trees are an incredible sight, the majority of them we have dubbed leadwood, it's incredibly dense and burns for an extremely long time as we found when we made ourselves a fire, a handful of logs could last hours on end, and you would often see the fire burning just as hot in the morning. There are others though, some with bright blue leaves, others with violent pink bark. The colours in this forest are amazing, and after nearly a week we're still amazed.

There's plants in the undergrowth that turn to face you as you walk past, keeping their vicious thorns towards you. A type of creeping plants like ivy that noticeably stab into their host tree, piercing the solid bark of even the leadwood trees. Other plants spread themselves along the ground as if they'd never even thought of going upwards, we tried following one of them to where it ended but the single plant seemed to cover miles of the undergrowth.

The fauna here are even more impressive. Back on the surface, above the drop, there are rarely any animals that don't have 4 limbs, with insects being the only real exception. This place has no such trend, with some animals not even having an even number of legs. There are tripods, pentapods and we've even seen a flying flatworm with about 30 wings. There are creatures with shells over an inch thick, they can curl up and become nearly indestructible. Some animals are stationary, they cement themselves into the twisting roots of trees and lash out at anything walking by with long tentacle like necks ending with a mouth that would make a needle factory envious. Steph was the unfortunate researcher that found out quite how dangerous these can be, the teeth point into the mouth, so the only way you can get away is to tear off your flesh. Her hand was left as a bloody mess.

That wasn't the only danger of this new forest, their seems to be a poisonous bat-like creature which leaves bites that don't naturally heal, only fester and spread necrotic tissue. You need to chop off the flesh containing the bite as soon as possible to avoid losing whole limbs to the ensuing corruption. There seem to be dangers greater than this too, with a group of 3 people going missing one day while fetching water from the nearby pool.

I should mention the pools, they're interesting too, they're perfectly round, about 20-30 or so yards across, but incredibly deep, we've thrown down glowsticks and we lose sight of them before they reach the bottom, and the water is nearly completely clear. When we first saw one Luke even made the joke 'Wanna try another descent?'.

Nights beneath the white sea are almost perfectly dark, daylight is reduced to twilight, but the light of the stars doesn't make a difference to the abyss of darkness the twilight forest becomes when the sun sets above the white sea. We've built a fence and nobody leaves the compound after dark, if the twilight forest is foreboding normally, the thought of tackling it by torchlight alone is terrifying.

Amazing, im loving everything about it.

The compound grew. chopping down the leadwood trees to make room was a monumental task though, it took hours to fell each one. People came from the city, we had military now, and We certainly needed it. 3 more groups had gone missing, a total of 13 people now, everybody was ill at ease because of it. The minimum group size had been bumped up to 5, with one of them being one of the armed military personnel.

We'd build a wall around the camp and even kept watch now during the night. Our biggest problem with the wall were the bark-eaters. They were a bit like centaurs, but they only had one arm, a giant, immensely strong arm that ended in a point. They also had a 3-part beak that could crush and eat the bark they strip off with their arm. Our wooden wall was easy pickings for them, so we had to keep them at bay during the night.

A few other people had fallen victim to the bats, we'd called them rot-bats for obvious reasons, they were too scared to cut off a whole chunk of their arm/leg/whatever, so ended up having to lose the whole thing. We've gotten better at spotting the root-dwellers, and after Steph there's only been one other incedent of those successfully attacking people.

We scouted along the drop and found the site of the eternal falls south of Tellac, where the mighty river Arul forever flows over the side, we could tell it was the one from the city because of the pollution in it. The trees surrounding the pool were strange and twisted, like the land there was somehow poisoned by this alien water. The river Arul carried on through the twilight forest, and the twisted trees also carried on growing by it's banks.

The bark-eaters left noticeable marks on the trees, giant patches with no bark, and this was fairly common throughout the forest, we just never knew what caused it before, but the twisted trees never had this, which seems strange, every other type of tree has fallen victim to them.

There's also been one of the round pools that had the twisted trees growing around it, we decided against drinking from it, and again none of the trees had been munched on, also none of them have the stabbing ivy. We're not entirely sure what to make of this yet but it's certainly peculiar. The water of the pool also had a more murky appearance, we took back a sample in one of our empty water bottles.

It was a military man that first tried to eat one of the creatures from down here, one of the bark-eaters that he shot he proceeded to roast up, oblivious to the potential dangers. As it turned out he was fine, but nobody else ate any for a few more days to see how he turned out, he was like an impromptu ginnea pig. Bark-eaters tasted like aniseed, but had a texture like extremely tough beef. Eating it was a strange experience, but it certainly seemed eadible, some people liked it more than others though, so we're still going to need most of our food to come from the surface.

We layed more cables on the drop, so now we have 2 cages that can be moved by making the one at the top heavy enough, like a fennicular railway. It's helped get some materials for more permanent huts, leadwood is far too hard to work with, and the other trees we found all have some other way to keep themselves intact, one of them bleeds a sap that would put the glue on the surface to shame, and another seems to heal it's core ridiculously quickly, so cutting all the way through is impossible.

The cause of the disappearances is still unknown, but most of us are too driven by curiosity to let that keep us away from the twilight forest.

White swirling fog draped itself around a young girl, the mist kissing her skin softly, forcing a shiver through her body. The only sound to be heard is the roaring of the feirce wind as it whips her hair and dress all around her face and body. Stepping closer to the precipice she wonders to herself if it would feel like a dream before it was over. Her sister calls out to her to stay safe and the girl only replies with a big smile and wave.

Thats when she noticed there was something not quite right,the fog wasn't moving on the wind but under its own accord. Faintly a low whistle like an old steam engine so far away it was barely audible. It was getting closer, and louder. Turning to where her sister was in a panic only to see her sister was no longer there.

“HEY!” she screamed, suddenly alone on the brink of tears, the whistle gaining momentum it seemed, ever louder, ever closer. Running as fast as her feet would carry her, lungs burning, eyes streaming with tears she sprints towards the village. The is fog thick now, the lights of town through the blanket of white billowing mist are all but invisible. Wiping the tears from her eyes, and swallowing her fear the girl suddenly stops the whistle now so loud its almost deafening.

Covering her ears wincing at the volume of the noise, she turns around to see a bright orange glow in the distance of the mist. Its getting closer notices the girl, now less afraid than confused. The light moves close, very close and the mist begins to be pushed away revealing a small freighter starship, glowing orange across its bottom hull with heat from re-entry into the atmosphere.

The girl wonders, is this why everyone left her alone? Why didn't they take her with them? What had she done wrong? Puzzled the girl accepted her fate and simply sat down on the damp ground. Her dress now a soaking wet mess of mud and lace.

The starship lands with a rush of pneumatic sounds, whirrs, large clunks and the droning whistle finally fades. With a loud metal on metal scraping, a hatch opens only to bathe the girl in a white-yellow light. A figure steps through the hatch only a sillouette of a man with body armour but no wepons. As he approaches the girl she can see he is smiling, this only serves to make her more uneasy.

The man makes his way down the slope of wet grass to the girl, still smiling and once close enough he finally speaks.

“You have been left behind, child.” He states “We will care for you, if you let us.”
